other_side: NLW's lead is that the frontier has got crowded and cheap — Grok 4.6 at sixty per cent less per token, Chinese open-weight models at a fraction of the price, and near-frontier performance now good enough for most work. Zitron's nearest engagement with that argument runs the other way: the industry cannot afford for AI to get cheaper, and the moment buyers saw real prices they flinched. He notes that "costs have only ever increased", and that ideas like efficiency "run counter to the greater narrative" because cheaper inference means less compute sold. His evidence is procurement, not benchmarks: Uber exhausted its annual token budget in a quarter and capped staff at $1,500 a month, T-Mobile at $2,000, Brex at $500 a week for engineers and $5 for everyone else. On the held-back-models point he is blunt — the labs "do not have some super secret trick up their sleeves" — and he dismisses benchmark-led capability claims outright.
truth_beneath: Both men orbit one variable: whether a falling price per unit of capability is real, or a narrative the sellers cannot afford to honour. They agree on more than the framing suggests — that the most expensive model is not what most work needs, that benchmarks are a poor guide, and that buyers are economising. The empirical question is whether the cost of a useful task keeps falling once discounting ends; the observable is per-task cost on real workloads, and enterprise token budgets rising rather than being capped. The residue is worldview: Whittemore reads cheap challengers as competition working, Zitron as a business with no floor under its pricing. Whittemore is vindicated if cheap near-frontier models take real production volume and total spend still grows; Zitron if the cuts prove promotional and per-task costs drift up. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain — and the signal is what they concede despite opposite priors: nobody needs the top model. Watch whether the next Ramp index shows cheap models taking share, or spend simply falling.
